text: What does Rice's theorem say, and what does it not cover?
choices: Every non-trivial property of a program's *behavior* is undecidable; properties of its *text* remain decidable.
Undecidable properties become decidable if the program is restricted to a finite input set.
Every property of a program is undecidable, including syntactic ones.
Only properties concerning termination are undecidable; others can be decided.
explanation: So there is no clever special case — not "is it correct", not "is it secure". But how many lines a program has, whether it uses `goto`, and whether the types check are all decidable. That is why compilers work: they analyse syntax, which is decidable, and cannot analyse behavior, which is not. Every static analysis tool lives on that line.
